scoreRule: 1 point per correct MC item; 10 points maximum; local provisional grade only
description: Independent C1 teacher-review bank for The Hidden Cost of Constant Improvement, with inferential and evaluative items, not approved.

tabs.title: Interpretation
tabs.description: Interpret the writer's argument and its implications.

tabs.title: Reasoning and qualifications
tabs.description: Evaluate how the writer qualifies their claims.

tabs.title: Critical transfer
tabs.description: Apply the argument to a new context.

questions.q: What is the writer's central concern about exhortations to improve?
choices: They tend to discourage schools from using assessment altogether.
They treat academic effort as less important than curiosity.
They are more motivating for high achievers than struggling learners.
They may transfer responsibility for obstacles onto individual students.
questions.explanation: The opening acknowledges growth can empower, but warns that improvement language may make every difficulty seem a student's personal failing.

questions.q: What is implied by the contrast between the two equally unsuccessful students?
choices: The same learning strategy will produce identical results under different conditions.
An identical outcome need not reflect an equivalent opportunity to succeed.
Equal grades prove that differences in resources have little effect.
Having an adult helper makes an assessment inherently unfair.
questions.explanation: Paragraph two deliberately holds performance equal while contrasting access to a quiet room, adult help and uninterrupted time.

questions.q: What does the example of a disagreement with a friend help establish?
choices: Learning can be meaningful even when no outcome can readily be quantified.
Debate is the only activity that develops genuine curiosity.
Social disagreement is more instructive than reading literature.
Progress is most valuable when both people change their views.
questions.explanation: The example demonstrates a gain in perspective that may not produce a measurable result.

questions.q: Which interpretation best captures 'choice more meaningful' in the conclusion?
choices: Individual responsibility begins only when all students have identical resources.
Students should choose their own assessment criteria without restrictions.
Practical support allows personal agency to operate under fairer conditions.
Schools should decide what choices will benefit students most.
questions.explanation: The author argues for institutional support that enables rather than replaces individual judgement.

questions.q: Why does the writer concede that growth-oriented ideas can be empowering?
choices: To establish that schools have largely solved the problem of poor grades.
To argue that positive posters are effective when used consistently.
To suggest that such ideas work only with young students.
To distinguish a useful principle from its potentially harmful application.
questions.explanation: The concession prevents a blanket rejection of perseverance while setting up a critique of encouragement unsupported by resources.

questions.q: Which assumption is challenged by the claim that advice cannot create a quiet room or an extra hour?
choices: Motivational advice can compensate for material obstacles by itself.
Students with difficult schedules are unwilling to change their habits.
Quiet environments do not influence independent study.
Students with supportive families do not need study strategies.
questions.explanation: The writer distinguishes advice about strategy from material resources that motivational language cannot supply.

questions.q: How does paragraph three broaden the argument beyond unequal access to study resources?
choices: It claims that curiosity can be measured more reliably than effort.
It questions the assumption that valuable experiences must show measurable improvement.
It recommends reducing compulsory assessment to a single final grade.
It suggests leisure activities should be planned like formal lessons.
questions.explanation: The paragraph adds concern that every activity, even leisure, is judged by a measurable-progress standard.

questions.q: A school introduces supervised study time but also tells pupils to revise their strategies. How would the writer probably view this?
choices: As useful only if schools stop giving grades for written work.
As ineffective unless every pupil achieves the same result.
As inconsistent, because practical support makes personal effort unnecessary.
As a constructive combination of support and individual responsibility.
questions.explanation: The concluding model pairs strategies chosen by learners with institutional support.

questions.q: A student enjoys a complex novel but cannot identify a measurable skill gained. Which response fits the argument?
choices: The novel counts as useful only if it directly improves examination results.
The experience matters chiefly because it provides leisure between assessments.
The reading may still have value even without a measurable improvement.
The student should read an easier text and record their speed.
questions.explanation: The writer argues that absorbing reading can be intrinsically valuable and resist measurement.

questions.q: Two pupils receive the same advice to work harder, but one lacks a quiet place to study. Which school response most closely follows the author's reasoning?
choices: Reward the first pupil publicly for using the available facilities.
Provide meaningful study access while retaining advice about effective strategies.
Give both students identical revision worksheets to ensure consistency.
Ask the second pupil to increase their motivation before seeking help.
questions.explanation: The writer proposes institutional resources such as supervised study spaces alongside personal learning strategies.
